headline: A deadly high-speed train crash in Spain, an attack at Israel's Belgrade embassy, and Merz in Tokyo

stories.title: Two high-speed trains collide south of Madrid, killing at least 30
facts: A Renfe AVE train with 397 passengers ran into the back of a stationary Iryo train with 146 passengers and a baby near Urda in Toledo province at 08:54 local time.
At least 30 people are dead and about 80 injured, and officials say the toll will very likely rise.
At least two carriages fell down an embankment, and the high-speed line between Madrid and Andalusia is closed.
RTVE reports the section was running on backup signalling (BSL) because of a fault in the main LZB train-protection system, with ASFA as the fallback.
The cause isn't confirmed yet. Spanish media are reporting both a possible signalling failure and possible human error.
It comes less than a year after the Adamuz crash in Córdoba province in January, which killed 46 people.
stories.whyItMatters: Spain runs Europe's largest high-speed network, and this is its second deadly crash in a year, so questions about the backup signalling will follow fast.

stories.title: Knife attacker shot dead outside Israel's embassy in Belgrade, and Serbia goes to red alert
facts: Just after midnight, a minor armed with two knives attacked a gendarmerie officer guarding the Israeli embassy, shouting "Allahu Akbar". The officer shot him dead.
The officer was cut on the left cheek. Prosecutors ruled the shooting self-defence.
Interior Minister Ivica Dačić says security services had been watching the attacker as a known Islamic State supporter, and he raised the terror threat level to red, the highest.
Israel's foreign ministry says no embassy staff were hurt, and the embassy was closed at the time.
It's the second attack on the embassy in under three years, after a crossbow attack on a guard in June 2024.

image.alt: A member of Serbia's Gendarmerie stands guard at the entrance to the Israeli embassy in Belgrade on October 28, 2026.

stories.title: Merz and Takaichi agree on economic security, and Merz floats a fighter jet with Japan
facts: On his first visit to Japan as chancellor, Merz and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi signed joint declarations on economic security and advanced technology.
They plan joint supply-chain monitoring and cooperation on rare earths, chips, batteries, EVs, industrial AI, robotics, pharma and wind, plus a memorandum on critical raw materials.
They're setting up a high-level dialogue on AI and want to work more closely on cyber defence.
Merz says Germany wants to explore building a combat aircraft with Japan and has commissioned a feasibility study.
He also proposed a "global political alliance for rules-based trade", including the WTO. The declarations implicitly criticise economic coercion by both China and the US.
Back home, the debate over who succeeds President Steinmeier has caught up with him. Ilse Aigner and Ines Claus are being discussed, and Merz is trying to slow it down.

stories.title: A 16-year-old bug in the UEFI reference code can let attackers run code before the OS boots
facts: CVE-2026-97631, rated 9.5 out of 10, is a buffer overflow in the PXE network-boot driver of TianoCore EDK II, the reference code most PC and server firmware builds on.
During a network boot, an oversized ICMP error message can overwrite memory and run code in ring 0, before Secure Boot and the TPM's protections take effect.
It was found by Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google, with disclosure planned for January. A public AMI pull request with the fix blew the embargo.
Exploiting it requires network access during the PXE boot window and has to be tailored to each firmware build. Machines that boot only from disk aren't affected.
Until vendors ship firmware updates, the advice is to turn off network boot where possible.

facts.text: Israel's count continues. With 84.5% of ballot boxes counted, Netanyahu's bloc is at 54 seats, Eisenkot's bloc at 49 and the Arab-led parties at 17. Around 600,000 double-envelope ballots may not be counted until Friday.

Zelensky is in The Hague, where he's meeting Prime Minister Rob Jetten and the King. The talks are about air defence against Shahed drones, and Jetten promises help with F-16 maintenance, spare parts and ammunition.
Microsoft has given Arkane Lyon, the Dishonored studio, until 13 December to find a buyer or partner. It is still working on Marvel's Blade.
Author Juli Zeh is stepping down early from the Brandenburg constitutional court, saying her writing makes the job hard to do. Her term would have run until 2029.
In Magdeburg, AfD politician Tobias Rausch may have been elected Saxony-Anhalt's Landtag president with CDU votes. CDU members are being asked to deny it in writing.

facts.text: The git, curl and python3 that ship with macOS still trust the compromised eMudhra certificates 11 days after Apple was told, and macOS 27.2 undid the manual workaround.

PortSwigger's Gareth Heyes bypassed six of eight popular SVG sanitizers, using XSLT data URLs, a Firefox Link header and Safari importing GIFs as SVG. Only DOMPurify and darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer held up.
Playwright MCP no longer marks test tools that run code or write files as read-only.
Evan You says work is underway to make OXC's parser three times faster.
pnpm says that a month into its zero-open-issues policy, fewer new issues are being filed each week.
Daniel Lemire writes about billion-query-per-second lookup tables in C++.
